checks.hint: set vm.swappiness=1 in /etc/sysctl.d/: at 60 the kernel swaps out database memory when the page cache grows
too much dirty data before write-back: checkpoints flush it in bursts that stall queries; set vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456 and vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824
always overcommit: under memory pressure the OOM killer kills a backend or the postmaster; use 2 (with vm.overcommit_ratio) or 0
disable THP for database hosts: compaction and khugepaged cause latency spikes; boot with transparent_hugepage=never or use a tuned profile that sets it

checks.value: none reserved; shared_buffers 25 % of RAM = 3.9 GiB
checks.hint: not needed below 8 GiB of shared_buffers; above that reserve vm.nr_hugepages
set vm.zone_reclaim_mode=0: otherwise the kernel drops local page cache instead of using memory on the other node
bfq is tuned for desktops and adds latency under a database load: use none or mq-deadline (udev rule or a tuned profile)
fine; noatime saves a few more writes
ext3 is outdated for a database: use xfs or ext4; every read updates the access time: mount with noatime
raise to 65536: LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit (services ignore limits.conf) or nofile in /etc/security/limits.d/
enough for one backend process per connection
the system-wide file limit is not a bottleneck
CPUs clock down between queries and add latency: use the performance governor (tuned profile throughput-performance, or cpupower frequency-set -g performance)
a power-saving profile: switch with tuned-adm profile throughput-performance

postgresql.why: 25 % of RAM: the rest stays for the OS page cache, which PostgreSQL also reads through
75 % of RAM: shared_buffers plus the page cache the planner can count on (no memory is allocated)
RAM / 16, at most 2GB: faster VACUUM and CREATE INDEX
(RAM - shared_buffers) / (max_connections 100 x 3): per sort or hash, so a query can use several; raise per session for reports
fewer, calmer checkpoints than the 1GB default; watch checkpoints_req in pg_stat_bgwriter / pg_stat_checkpointer
a quarter of max_wal_size: WAL files are recycled instead of created
spread checkpoint writes over 90 % of the interval (default since PostgreSQL 14)
SSD/NVMe (non-rotational disks detected): a random read costs about the same as a sequential one, so index scans get chosen
SSD/NVMe (non-rotational disks detected): many I/O requests in flight for bitmap heap scans
one per CPU (8), at least the default 8
half the CPUs, at most 4: one query must not take every core
half the CPUs, at most 4, for CREATE INDEX
use huge pages once vm.nr_hugepages=2090 is reserved; falls back to normal pages until then
more than 4 x CPUs (32) busy at once only queue for CPU: if most connections are active, put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front
